corrected_value.title: Precursors and Mediators of Intergroup Reconciliation in Northern Ireland: A New Model.

decisions.quote:
This article aims to replicate, refine and extend the Rec-
onciliation Orientation Model (ROM; Noor et al. 2008a), which
examines key intergroup conflict factors – such as competitive
victimhood, ingroup identity and forgiveness.
decisions.location: Section 1 Introduction, p. 1354, lines 79-82 (and References, p. 1366, lines 1738-1740)
decisions.reason: The paper cites two 2008 sibling papers by Noor and Brown in the reference list (lines 1738-1744): Noor, Brown, and Prentice (2008a, British Journal of Social Psychology) and Noor, Brown, Gonzalez, Manzi, and Lewis (2008b, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin). Shipped row 1285 mistakenly linked Noor et al. (2008b), which is cited only once in passing as supporting literature on Chile's Pinochet regime (Section 1.1, line 149). Throughout the text (lines 79-82, 90-92, 153-157, 397-399, 463-465, 556-557, 929-930, 959, 1101-1102), the authors explicitly identify Noor et al. (2008a) on the Reconciliation Orientation Model (ROM) in Northern Ireland as the original study being replicated. Blind coding (target_index 0) identified the right original.

decisions.quote:
Testing the refined and
extended ROM in four real-life conflict settings demonstrated that
the more group members engage in competitive victimhood, the
less forgiving they are of their past grievances.
These findings replicate the results reported by the original test
of ROM (Noor et al. 2008a) and related literature (Uluğ et al.
2021).
decisions.reason: Evaluating the outcome for the resolved original study (Noor et al. 2008a), the authors explicitly state an overall verdict that their findings replicate the original test of ROM (Noor et al. 2008a), confirming the negative effect of competitive victimhood on intergroup forgiveness, partial mediation via ingroup identity, and the superior fit of identity as mediator over the reverse mediation model (lines 929-944, 1085-1103). The contrasting positive path for self-definition (after accounting for suppression by self-investment) and moderation by conflict type are presented as refinements and extensions to ROM rather than replication failures.

decisions.quote:
This research replicated, refined and extended the Reconciliation Orientation Model (ROM). While the original ROM treated
ingroup identity as unidimensional, we adopted a multidimensional model, distinguishing self-investment and self-definition, and
examined their links to intergroup forgiveness. Data from four real-life conflict settings – Israeli–Palestinian, Kosovar–Serbian,
US racial and UK gender conflict (N = 860) – showed good fit for the refined ROM.
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind codings agree that the study is a replication. The authors collected new survey data (N = 860 across four intergroup conflict settings) to re-test the Reconciliation Orientation Model (ROM; Noor et al. 2008a).
